```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(ggplot2)
  library(knitr)
})

kOutputDir <- file.path("..", "output", "omip43")

ReadOutput <- function(name) {
  path <- file.path(kOutputDir, name)
  if (!file.exists(path)) {
    stop(
      "The analysis output is missing: ", path, "\n",
      "Run scripts/06_omip43_asc_analysis.R first."
    )
  }
  read.csv(path, check.names = FALSE)
}

OutputImage <- function(name) {
  file.path(kOutputDir, name)
}
```

## Why this dataset

OMIP-043 identifies antibody secreting cells, historically called plasma cells,
across four human tissues [1]. The target population is defined as CD38 high and
CD27 positive. CD38 high is the bright end of a continuous distribution rather
than a separated peak. A method that looks for a dip between two peaks requires
verification on this panel.

The authors state a design target in counting terms. Both halves of that
statement can be tested against the deposited data. The analysis reproduces the
paper's findings as closely as the deposited data allows.

### What the replicates are

Each tissue group holds seven files that share one `$SRC` and one acquisition
date, 3 August 2017. They are replicate acquisitions of one preparation per
tissue and not seven donors. Donor variation is absent, so the spread across the
seven files measures acquisition and analysis.

## Methods

### The dataset

FlowRepository accession FR-FCM-Z2ZG (OMIP-043) contains flow cytometry files
from four human tissues: blood, bone marrow, spleen and tonsil. Each tissue
group holds seven replicate files from one preparation, acquired on 3 August
2017. The target population is antibody secreting cells, defined as CD38 high
and CD27 positive.

### Preprocessing

FCS files were read and compensation was applied using the spillover matrix
stored in the SPILL keyword. Fluorescence channels were transformed to a logicle
scale.

### Gating

The deposited FlowJo workspace defines seven sequential populations: a time
gate, a viability gate, a permissive scatter gate, two singlet gates, a dump
gate for CD3, CD14, CD15 and CD193, and the ASC gate on CD38 and CD27. The
manual ASC gate is a rectangleGate on CD38 from 141.8 to 209.1 and on CD27 from
109.7 to 211.3.

An automated gating template was constructed to mirror the manual hierarchy.
Density minimum gating (mindensity) was applied to the viability and dump gates,
and two sequential mindensity gates were used to reach CD38 high.

### Statistics

The coefficient of variation from counting alone follows a Poisson distribution,
calculated as 1 divided by the square root of the event count. The measured CV
across replicates was compared against this floor.

FlowSOM clustering was performed with 15 metaclusters. Clusters were scored
against the manual ASC gate using purity and recall. A configuration sweep
tested 48 combinations of metacluster count, scatter channel inclusion, channel
scaling, and selection rule. Each configuration was ranked on its worst tissue
F1 score.

Cluster annotation used a definitions file specifying expected marker signs for
each cell type. Median marker expression per cluster was scaled to 0 to 1 and
scored against the definitions.

### Software

The analysis used R with the flowCore, openCyto, FlowSOM, and ggplot2 packages.
Every version is pinned in the container and asserted at build time.

## Part 1: the manual gates

The manual ASC gate was applied to each of the 28 files through the deposited
workspace.

```{r}
#| label: manual-counts

manual <- ReadOutput("manual_asc_counts.csv")
kable(
  manual[, c("tissue", "parent_events", "asc_events", "asc_percent",
             "poisson_cv_percent")],
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Every replicate. The parent is the dumped population, which is what the paper uses as its denominator.",
  col.names = c("Tissue", "Parent events", "ASC events", "ASC percent",
                "Poisson CV percent")
)
```

ASC frequencies range from 0.23 percent in blood to 3.5 percent in spleen. The
seven replicates within each tissue show close agreement.

## Part 2: the counting claims

The paper states its design target directly.

> We targeted a 5% coefficient of variation (CV), which resulted in regularly
> collecting 400-2,000 events in the ASC gate.

The two numbers in that sentence are linked by arithmetic. A count of rare
events follows a Poisson distribution, so the relative spread from counting
alone is `1 / sqrt(n)`. At 400 events that spread is 5 percent.

```{r}
#| label: counting-claims

counting <- ReadOutput("counting_claims.csv")
kable(
  counting,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "The paper's two targets, checked against its own data.",
  col.names = c("Tissue", "Mean events", "All in 400 to 2000",
                "Replicates in range", "Poisson CV percent", "Meets 5 percent CV")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: count-plot
#| fig-cap: "Events in the ASC gate. The band is the paper's stated range."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("asc_event_counts.png"))
```

None of the 28 replicates falls inside the stated 400 to 2,000 range. Blood and
bone marrow sit below it at 290 and 185 events. Spleen and tonsil sit above it
at around 3,500. The word "regularly" in the quoted sentence describes the
authors' usual practice across many experiments rather than a promise about this
deposit. The 5 percent CV target is met in spleen and tonsil and missed in blood
and bone marrow.

### The floor and what sits above it

The measured CV across the seven replicates includes the Poisson counting floor
plus pipetting, staining, acquisition and the gate.

```{r}
#| label: spread

spread <- ReadOutput("asc_spread.csv")
kable(
  spread,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "The counting floor against what seven replicates actually did.",
  col.names = c("Tissue", "Replicates", "Mean count", "Mean percent",
                "Poisson CV percent", "Measured CV percent", "Excess CV percent")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: cv-plot
#| fig-cap: "The two coefficients of variation, by tissue."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("cv_comparison.png"))
```

The excess CV column shows the measured spread minus the Poisson floor. In
blood, bone marrow and spleen the measured spread sits above the counting floor.
In tonsil the measured CV of 1.17 percent falls below the Poisson floor of 1.73
percent, and the excess is reported as missing rather than as a negative number.

A measured spread below the counting floor is not possible for independent
samples, so the seven tonsil files are not independent. They are repeated
acquisitions from one tube, where the same cells can be sampled more than once
and the counts are correlated.

## Part 3: automated gating, and why it fails

The template mirrors the manual hierarchy, with `mindensity` for the viability
and dump gates and two sequential `mindensity` gates to reach CD38 high.

```{r}
#| label: template

template <- read.csv(
  file.path("..", "gating", "omip43_gating_template.csv"),
  check.names = FALSE
)
kable(
  template[, c("alias", "pop", "parent", "dims", "gating_method", "gating_args")],
  caption = "The template. It runs without error and the answer is wrong."
)
```

```{r}
#| label: automated

automated <- ReadOutput("automated_vs_manual.csv")
kable(
  automated[, c("tissue", "asc_percent_manual", "asc_percent_automated",
                "fold_error")],
  digits = 3,
  caption = "The template against the manual mean, one replicate per tissue.",
  col.names = c("Tissue", "Manual percent", "Automated percent", "Fold error")
)
```

This result is worse than a wrong answer. The template is wrong in both
directions, and by a different amount in each tissue. It undercounts bone marrow
threefold and it overcounts spleen eighteenfold. A method that is consistently
wrong can be corrected. A method whose error changes sign between tissues cannot
be trusted anywhere.

### What the gate is, read from the workspace

The manual ASC gate is a `rectangleGate` on CD38 from 141.8 to 209.1 and on CD27
from 109.7 to 211.3. A human placed that box, using knowledge of where these
cells sit. It is a threshold decision and not a boundary that the data
announces, and the paper says as much in its own words.

> On-scale display of CD38high events is critical for ASC identification, and can
> be difficult for the untrained eye.

## Part 3b: where a density method actually cuts

The section above shows that the template is wrong, but it does not show why,
and the obvious explanation deserves a test rather than an assertion.
`mindensity` was therefore run on the CD38 channel of exactly the data the
analyst looked at, in the workspace's own scale, and its threshold was compared
with theirs.

```{r}
#| label: cd38-thresholds

thresholds <- ReadOutput("cd38_thresholds.csv")
kable(
  thresholds,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Where each method cuts CD38, on the same events, in the same scale.",
  col.names = c("Tissue", "Analyst threshold", "mindensity threshold",
                "Percent above analyst", "Percent above mindensity",
                "Manual ASC percent")
)
```

The table corrects the simple story. In spleen the two methods almost agree, at
144.2 against 141.8, which gives 3.48 percent of events above the cut against
3.59 percent. A single density gate on CD38 would have been close to right
there. In the other three tissues `mindensity` cuts far too low, at 80, 73 and
84 against analyst thresholds of 124, 128 and 142. It keeps 27, 35 and 14
percent of events where the analyst kept 3.1, 0.8 and 0.9 percent.

The method is therefore not blind. It succeeds where the target population is
abundant enough to bend the density curve, which in spleen means 3.3 percent of
events, and it fails where the population is rare, which in the other three
tissues means 0.3 to 0.9 percent. The rarer the cell, the less of a feature it
leaves for a density method to find, and this is a rare cell panel.

```{r}
#| label: cd38-density
#| fig-cap: "Spleen. The solid line is the analyst's threshold, the dashed line is where mindensity cuts."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("cd38_density.png"))
```

The figure shows what the arithmetic says. There is one large mode and a long
shoulder, and `mindensity` finds the dip between negative and positive rather
than the start of the bright tail.

```{r}
#| label: cd38-biaxial
#| fig-cap: "The plot the analyst drew on. The red box is their gate, the dashed line is the density cut."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("cd38_cd27_biaxial.png"))
```

The analyst's gate also has an upper bound on both markers. A density threshold
has no upper bound at all, so the two gates are not the same object even where
the lower edges agree.

## Part 4: clustering recovers what gating missed

Clustering does not need a valley. It groups events by their position in all
seven markers at once, and ASC differ from everything around them on several of
those markers together. They are CD38 bright, CD27 positive, CD20 low and side
scatter high. The manual gate is used here only to score the result, and the
clustering never sees it.

```{r}
#| label: clustering

clustering <- ReadOutput("clustering_summary.csv")
kable(
  clustering,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "FlowSOM with 15 metaclusters, scored against the manual ASC gate.",
  col.names = c("Tissue", "Manual ASC", "Manual percent", "Best cluster purity",
                "Best cluster recall", "ASC clusters", "Combined recall",
                "Combined percent")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: umap-manual
#| fig-cap: "Spleen. Red is the ASC gate the authors drew. The embedding was built without it."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("umap_spleen_manual.png"))
```

```{r}
#| label: umap-clusters
#| fig-cap: "The same embedding, coloured by metacluster."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("umap_spleen_clusters.png"))
```

In three of the four tissues a single metacluster is over 91 percent ASC, and
recall runs from 72 to 95 percent. In spleen a second cluster takes the combined
recall to 97.4 percent. Blood is the weakest case at 63.2 percent purity, and
that result is expected. With 165 ASC among 50,000 events, the population is too
small to hold a metacluster of its own, so it shares one with its nearest
neighbours.

### How each metacluster was labelled

Purity and recall say whether a cluster matches the manual gate. They do not say
what any cluster is, and FlowSOM returns fifteen numbered groups and nothing
else. No cluster was named by eye. The naming rule lives in a file and runs in
four steps, and the first step is to write down what each cell type looks like.
The definitions file gives the expected sign of each marker for each type, as
`pos`, `neg`, `high`, or blank when the marker does not take part.

```{r}
#| label: definitions

definitions <- read.csv(
  file.path("..", "gating", "omip43_cell_type_definitions.csv"),
  check.names = FALSE
)

# The file names detectors, because that is what the score has to match against
# the data. Here the columns are shown as markers, so this table and the scaled
# table below can be read side by side.
detector_to_marker <- c(
  "Comp-APC-A" = "CD19",
  "Comp-BV421-A" = "CD20",
  "Comp-PerCP-Cy5-5-A" = "IgD",
  "Comp-BV786-A" = "CD27",
  "Comp-BUV395-A" = "CD38"
)
shown <- definitions
names(shown)[match(names(detector_to_marker), names(shown))] <- detector_to_marker

kable(
  shown[, c("cell_type", unname(detector_to_marker))],
  caption = "The definitions the labels are scored against. A blank means the marker takes no part in that type."
)
```

The reasoning behind each row is kept in the file itself, in a `note` column
that the table above leaves out for width.

```{r}
#| label: definition-notes

kable(
  definitions[, c("cell_type", "note")],
  caption = "Why each definition is written that way.",
  col.names = c("Cell type", "Note")
)
```

Five markers do the labelling. The clustering itself used seven, adding
cytoplasmic immunoglobulin and HLA-DR, so the scaled table below carries two
columns that the score does not read. Those two are shown because they help a
reader judge a label even when the rule ignores them. The second step takes the
median of every marker in every cluster and scales it. Each marker is rescaled
to run from 0 to 1 across the fifteen clusters, so a bright marker and a dim one
carry equal weight, and the score reads this table rather than the raw medians.

```{r}
#| label: scaled-expression

scaled <- ReadOutput("spleen_cluster_scaled_expression.csv")
kable(
  scaled,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Median expression per cluster, scaled from 0 to 1 within each marker. This is the table the score reads."
)
```

The third step scores every cluster against every definition. For each marker
the definition names, the rule adds the scaled value where it expects `pos`,
twice the scaled value where it expects `high`, and one minus the scaled value
where it expects `neg`, then divides by the total weight. The division matters.
An earlier version summed instead, which rewards a definition for the number of
markers it names rather than for the fit, and the label with the longest marker
list then wins clusters it has no business winning. The last step takes the best
score and records how close the second was. That gap is the margin, and it is
the part of the output that says how much to trust the label.

```{r}
#| label: cluster-annotation

annotation <- ReadOutput("spleen_cluster_annotation.csv")
kable(
  annotation[, c("cluster", "events", "percent_of_total", "cell_type",
                 "runner_up", "margin", "asc_percent_by_manual_gate")],
  digits = 3,
  caption = "The fifteen metaclusters, their label, the runner up, and the gap between them.",
  col.names = c("Cluster", "Events", "Percent", "Label", "Runner up", "Margin",
                "ASC percent by the manual gate")
)
```

### Whether the labels are any good

The last two columns check each other, and they were produced without any shared
information. The label comes from marker expression scored against a definitions
file, and the final column comes from a gate an analyst drew in FlowJo. Cluster
4 is labelled antibody secreting cells with a margin of 0.409, and the manual
gate calls 91.7 percent of its events ASC. Cluster 3 gets the same label with a
margin of 0.136, and the gate agrees on 60.3 percent. Two independent routes
reach the same conclusion.

Read the scaled table for cluster 4 and the label is obvious without any
arithmetic. CD38 is at 1.00, CD27 is at 1.00, and CD20 is at 0.02. That is the
highest CD38 in the panel, CD27 positive, and CD20 switched off, which is the
paper's definition of an ASC.

Five of the fifteen labels carry a margin below 0.1, and a reader should treat
those as undecided rather than as answers. Two of the five are informative.
Cluster 12 has CD19 at 0.93 and CD20 at 0.90, with IgD at 0.06 and CD27 at 0.12,
so it is a B cell that is neither IgD positive nor CD27 positive. Cluster 14 has
IgD at 0.78 and CD27 at 0.64, so it is positive for both. Neither state is in
the definitions file, and the low margins are the method reporting the gap
rather than hiding it.

Cluster 7 is the one clear error. It is labelled antibody secreting cells and
the manual gate calls 0.7 percent of it ASC. Its margin is 0.045, so the label
is wrong and the margin says so.

### What had to be corrected

The first version of the definitions file required memory B cells to be positive
for cytoplasmic immunoglobulin and for HLA-DR. On this panel the FITC channel
carries cytoplasmic Ig, which is high on ASC and low elsewhere, and HLA-DR
varies. Those two requirements pulled the memory B score down far enough that
cluster 13 was labelled non-B by a margin of 0.007, on a cluster that holds 16.7
percent of the file with CD19 at 0.96, CD20 at 0.77, CD27 at 0.74 and IgD at
0.14. The definitions were cut back to the markers that actually define these
subsets, which are CD19, CD20, IgD, CD27 and CD38, and cluster 13 is now
labelled memory B cells with a margin of 0.240.

The correction is recorded here rather than applied quietly, because the method
did not fail in that first run. The definitions did, and the margin of 0.007
flagged it before anyone looked at the biology.

Set against the manual values, the frequencies the clustering produces are
close. Spleen gives 4.03 percent against 3.34, tonsil gives 0.77 against 0.86,
and bone marrow gives 0.43 against 0.45. Those values are within a factor of
1.2. The template was out by a factor of 18.

## Part 5: the phenotype claims

```{r}
#| label: phenotype

phenotype <- ReadOutput("phenotype.csv")
kable(
  phenotype[, c("tissue", "ssc_asc", "ssc_other", "ssc_ratio")],
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Median side scatter of ASC against the rest of the dumped population.",
  col.names = c("Tissue", "ASC", "Other cells", "Ratio")
)
```

The paper warns about the scatter position of these cells.

> ASC contain more cytoplasm due to their active production of antibody, and thus
> do not cluster with a typical low-side scatter "lymphocyte" gate.

The claim reproduces in all four tissues. ASC scatter 1.8 to 2.7 times more
light than the cells around them. The claim also has a direct consequence for
automated gating, and it is the reason the template above uses a permissive
`boundary` gate on scatter rather than a `flowClust` lymphocyte gate. A
conventional lymphocyte gate would have removed much of the target population
before any marker was looked at, and the analysis would have run to completion
and reported a number.

```{r}
#| label: cd20

kable(
  phenotype[, c("tissue", "cd20_asc", "cd20_other", "cd20_difference")],
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Median CD20 on ASC against the rest of the dumped population.",
  col.names = c("Tissue", "ASC", "Other cells", "Difference")
)
```

> Mature B cells express the phosphoglycoproteins CD19 and CD20, and on
> differentiation to ASCs, CD20 is downregulated.

The claim reproduces in all four tissues, with the difference from 7 to 38
units.

```{r}
#| label: tissue-variation

kable(
  phenotype[, c("tissue", "cd19_asc", "hladr_asc", "cd38_asc")],
  digits = 1,
  caption = "Median intensity among ASC only, by tissue.",
  col.names = c("Tissue", "CD19", "HLA-DR", "CD38")
)

variation <- ReadOutput("tissue_variation.csv")
kable(
  variation,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Spread of the ASC median across the four tissues.",
  col.names = c("Marker", "CV across tissues, percent")
)
```

> The ratio of CD19+ to CD19- on ASC varies by tissue niche.

CD19 varies across tissues among ASC, from 127 in bone marrow to 165 in tonsil,
and the direction matches the literature the paper cites, where CD19 negative
ASC are enriched in bone marrow. The paper also names Ki67 as a marker that
varies by tissue. That claim cannot be tested here, because the PE channel in
these deposited files carries HLA-DR and not Ki67. The paper describes both as
options for that channel. The claim is recorded as not measurable rather than as
failed.

## Part 6: every claim, with a verdict

The sections above measure. This one decides, so that no claim in the file is
left without an answer. The seven claims live in
`gating/omip43_paper_claims.csv`, each with the sentence it came from, so a
reader can check the claim against the paper before checking the number against
the data.

```{r}
#| label: claims-file

claims <- read.csv(
  file.path("..", "gating", "omip43_paper_claims.csv"),
  check.names = FALSE
)
kable(
  claims[, c("claim_id", "short_name", "measure", "test", "figure")],
  caption = "The claims as recorded. The quote column holds the sentence each came from and is left out here for width."
)
```

```{r}
#| label: verdicts

verdicts <- ReadOutput("claims_verdicts.csv")
kable(
  verdicts[, c("claim_id", "short_name", "expected", "observed", "verdict")],
  caption = "Each claim against the deposited data.",
  col.names = c("Claim", "Short name", "Paper expects", "Observed", "Verdict")
)
```

Five of the seven claims reproduce cleanly. The two that do not are both
counting claims, and neither is a failure of the biology. Claim 2 fails
outright, because no replicate falls in the stated 400 to 2,000 range. Claim 3
is met in spleen and tonsil and missed in blood and bone marrow. Both claims
come from the same sentence, and both track the same thing, which is how rare
the cells are in a given tissue.

One claim could not be tested at all. The paper names Ki67 alongside CD19 and
HLA-DR as markers that vary between tissues, but the PE channel in these
deposited files carries HLA-DR rather than Ki67. The paper describes both as
options for that channel, so the claim is recorded here as not measurable rather
than counted as a failure, because the data to test it was never deposited.

### The same claims, from a population the manual gate never touched

Everything above defines ASC by the gate the authors drew. That asks whether the
paper's conclusions follow from its own analysis, which is worth knowing and is
not the same as an independent reproduction. The population was therefore
rebuilt from scratch. Each tissue was clustered, the clusters that carry the
highest median CD38 were taken as the population, and the manual gate was not
consulted at any point.

```{r}
#| label: cluster-route

cluster_route <- ReadOutput("cluster_route_phenotype.csv")
kable(
  cluster_route[, c("tissue", "asc_clusters", "asc_percent", "manual_percent",
                    "agreement_percent", "ssc_ratio", "cd20_difference")],
  digits = 2,
  caption = "ASC defined by clustering alone, against the manual value for the same file.",
  col.names = c("Tissue", "Clusters used", "Clustering percent", "Manual percent",
                "Agreement percent", "Side scatter ratio", "CD20 difference")
)
```

All four tissues land close. Bone marrow gives 0.42 percent against 0.45, spleen
gives 2.90 against 3.34, tonsil gives 0.68 against 0.86, and blood gives 0.49
against 0.33. Agreement on which individual events are selected runs from 64.5
percent in blood to 95.1 percent in bone marrow.

```{r}
#| label: both-routes

both <- ReadOutput("claims_both_routes.csv")
kable(
  both[, c("claim_id", "short_name", "route", "observed", "verdict")],
  caption = "Each claim by both routes. The two counting claims can only be tested on gated counts, so they appear once.",
  col.names = c("Claim", "Short name", "Route", "Observed", "Verdict")
)
```

Four of the five claims that clustering can test reproduce by clustering, with
the same directions and comparable magnitudes as the authors' own gates. The
fifth fails on a margin of 0.07 percentage points, and the next section explains
why that verdict is kept rather than tuned away.

### Getting there took two attempts, and the first one failed

The first version of this route selected clusters by a score of their whole
marker profile against a definitions file. It worked in tonsil and spleen, and
it failed badly in bone marrow, where it called 9.44 percent of the parent ASC
against a manual gate of 0.45, with only 4.1 percent of the selected events
inside that gate. The numbers said where to look. Precision in bone marrow was 4
to 7 percent while recall was 87 to 99, so the target cells were found and then
diluted in a cluster far too large to be ASC. That is not a clustering problem.
It is the rule that decides which cluster to keep.

Forty-eight configurations were then measured across all four tissues. They
varied the number of metaclusters, whether scatter channels join the clustering,
whether channels are scaled, and the selection rule. Each configuration was
ranked on its worst tissue rather than on its average, because an average hides
a total failure.

```{r}
#| label: sweep-by-rule

sweep_summary <- ReadOutput("clustering_sweep_summary.csv")
by_rule <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  c("profile", "cd38 top 1", "cd38 top 2", "cd38 top 3"),
  function(rule) {
    piece <- sweep_summary[sweep_summary$selection == rule, ]
    data.frame(
      selection = rule,
      configurations = nrow(piece),
      best_worst_f1 = max(piece$worst_f1),
      median_worst_f1 = stats::median(piece$worst_f1),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  }
))
kable(
  by_rule,
  digits = 1,
  caption = "The selection rule, summarised over every combination of the other three settings.",
  col.names = c("Selection rule", "Configurations", "Best worst-tissue F1",
                "Median worst-tissue F1")
)
```

The selection rule decides everything, and the other three settings barely
matter. Every profile configuration lands between 6.8 and 12.2 on its worst
tissue. Every configuration that ranks on CD38 and takes the top one lands
between 48.7 and 77.1. The reason is in the paper, and it is not in the
parameters.

> ASC also express very high levels of the ectoenzyme CD38 and are positive for the
> TNF-family receptor CD27. Very high CD38 expression is in fact considered
> adequate for basic identification of ASC.

The population is defined by one marker at an extreme value, and not by the
shape of a profile. Three clusters are worse than one, at a best worst-tissue F1
of 10.0, because the third admits a population that is positive without being
extreme.

```{r}
#| label: sweep-top

kable(
  head(sweep_summary, 8),
  digits = 1,
  caption = "The eight best configurations. The chosen one is the first row.",
  col.names = c("Metaclusters", "Scatter", "Scaled", "Selection", "Mean F1",
                "Worst F1", "Worst tissue")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: selection-rule

improvement <- ReadOutput("clustering_improvement.csv")
kable(
  improvement,
  digits = 1,
  caption = "The first configuration against the chosen one, scored against the manual gate.",
  col.names = c("Tissue", "First precision", "First recall", "First F1",
                "Chosen precision", "Chosen recall", "Chosen F1")
)
```

Bone marrow goes from the worst tissue to the best, at 95.1 percent agreement.

### The trade-off the sweep exposed

The top two clusters reproduce all five claims, and they agree less well with
the manual gate, at a worst-tissue F1 of 69.6 against 77.1. The top one cluster
agrees better and it loses claim 1. This report keeps the sweep winner, so claim
1 fails on the clustering route, and the reason is worth seeing rather than
switching to whichever rule scores better on the claim table.

Claim 1 says that ASC are rarest in blood. By the manual gate that is clear, at
0.26 percent in blood against 0.41 in bone marrow. By the clustering route the
two values are 0.49 and 0.42, so bone marrow comes out marginally lower and the
ordering flips. The two tissues sit 0.07 percentage points apart. That gap is
smaller than the difference between the clustering route and the manual gate in
either tissue on its own, so the method cannot resolve it, and a verdict of
reproduced would have been luck rather than evidence.

### What this step is and is not

The manual gate was used to score the configurations above, which makes this a
calibration step rather than an independent test. A choice of method by how well
it matches a reference is legitimate. A claim that the result is independent
afterwards would not be. What survives that objection is the reasoning. The rule
was not found by a search for whatever matched best. It was taken from a
sentence in the paper, and the sweep then confirmed that every rule which
ignores that sentence performs six times worse.

```{r}
#| label: verdict-summary

summary_table <- as.data.frame(table(verdicts$verdict))
colnames(summary_table) <- c("verdict", "claims")
kable(summary_table, caption = "The seven claims, summarised.")
```

## Discussion

### The failure is silent, which is the part that matters

The template ran to completion on every tissue. It raised no error, it produced
a population, and it reported a percentage. Nothing in the output said that the
CD38 high gate had kept everything handed to it. That is the risk in an
automated pipeline, and it is worse than a crash. A crash stops you. A number
does not.

The check that caught it here is cheap and general. Compare the automated result
against a gate somebody drew by hand, on the same file, before you trust the
pipeline on files nobody has looked at.

### Rarity is what breaks the density method

Part 3b separates two explanations that are easy to confuse. The first is that
CD38 high has no density valley at all. That is not quite true. In spleen a
single `mindensity` cut lands at 144.2 against the analyst's 141.8, and it keeps
3.48 percent of events against their 3.59 percent. The second explanation is
that the population must be abundant enough to leave a feature in the density
curve, and that is what the data supports. Spleen holds 3.3 percent ASC and the
method works. Blood, bone marrow and tonsil hold 0.3 to 0.9 percent, and the cut
falls 40 to 60 units too low, so it keeps 14 to 35 percent of events instead of
about 1 to 3 percent.

The rule is therefore not that density gating cannot find a bright tail. The
rule is that a density method needs the population to be common enough to bend
the curve, and a rare cell panel is precisely the case where it is not.

### Why clustering does better here

Clustering never looks for a valley on one axis. It groups events by their
position across all seven markers at once, and ASC differ from their neighbours
on four of them together. They are CD38 bright, CD27 positive, CD20 low and side
scatter high. That is why the clustering route lands within a factor of 1.5 of
the manual value in all four tissues, including bone marrow at 0.42 percent
against 0.45, where the density gate was out by threefold in the other
direction. The two automated routes do not fail together. The density gate
failed in three tissues of four, and the clustering route failed in none once
its selection rule matched the paper's own definition.

It took two attempts to get there, and the first attempt failed in bone marrow
for a reason worth carrying forward. A rare population does not claim a cluster
of its own, so the rule that picks which cluster to keep matters more than the
clustering parameters. Across all 48 configurations, every rule that scored the
whole marker profile stayed below an F1 of 12.2 on its worst tissue, and every
rule that ranked on CD38 and took the top cluster reached 48.7 or better.

### What this shows and what it does not

What this analysis shows is that an automated template can fail silently on a
published panel, that the failure tracks how rare the target population is, and
that a different automated method recovers the same cells without hand tuning.
It does not show that clustering is safe. The selection rule that made it work
was chosen with the manual gate in hand, so this is a calibrated method rather
than an independent one, and blood still agrees on only 64.5 percent of the
events it selects. It does not measure analyst variation either. Seven replicate
acquisitions of one tube are not seven analysts, and the tonsil result, where
the measured CV fell below the Poisson floor, shows that those replicates are
not fully independent of one another. What the arithmetic did show is worth
keeping. A measured spread that falls below the counting floor is a statement
about the study design rather than about the biology, and one line of Poisson
arithmetic was enough to see it.

## Reproducing this

```bash
# Pull this dataset only, 2.6 GB of the 103 GB archive
./sync.sh pull datasets/flowrepository/OMIP-43

# Build the container. Every package version is pinned and asserted at build time.
./containers/build.sh

# The analysis
podman run --rm -v "$PWD:/work:z" -w /work everything-flow-cytometry:latest \
  Rscript scripts/06_omip43_asc_analysis.R

# This report
podman run --rm -v "$PWD:/work:z" -w /work everything-flow-cytometry:latest \
  quarto render reports/omip43_asc_analysis.qmd
```
